text:
And the little horse trotted on; the little horse, insensible to the warmth of spring, equally weary and resigned in the storms of winter and in the dog days of summer, limped over the hostile stones, slowly, slowly, with that immovable philosophy which comes after despair; a poor old machine made of bones and aches, indifferent to the tugs, the lashes, the impatience of the customers, as though by now it knew that its entire destiny was to keep going, by dint of stumbling and wheezing, slowly, but to keep going.

The nearby countryside sent a few rural scents among the last houses, and already appeared entirely open, almost wrapped in a violet air, along the side roads that were no longer paved. The driver turned into one of them.

“I have never come this far,” Loretta said. “It feels as though we are in the country; smell how lovely it is!”

Some meadow nearby had been mown; the haymaking stacks gave off vegetal fragrances in the spring evening. Even the nag, at that scent of savory May hay, seemed to feel its greedy soul swell within its lean flanks, and pulled harder. The driver stuck a cigar stub between his teeth and began to hum; with cracks of his whip he accompanied his monotonous singsong. This made Loretta laugh.

“How funny he is!” she said softly to her brother. And she drew close to him with a little laugh that breathed her fresh breath into his face.

He did not speak; a sort of torpor, a sensation he had never known, gently enveloped his spirit, imparting to him a physical weariness, a kind of sensual languor. For one brief hour he liked to forget that his little companion, she whose arm it was sweet to feel beneath his arm and whose breath upon his face, was his very own sister, come from the same womb that had given him life, nourished with the same milk, rocked in the same cradle: the daughter of his father and his mother, his full sister.

At the same time he felt an immense horror, an unconscious horror, of himself, and yet in this he found his greatest voluptuous pleasure. He liked to hear her speak; that voice, which he felt he had never known before, entered the innermost depths of his heart, lavishing upon him something like a slow and exhausting caress. That she said she loved him, that she dared tell him that she loved him, that her desire was so manifest to him, so ready to let itself be seized, that she had an almost morbid need to wrap herself around his person and make him feel the trembling of her soft, still untouched limbs, that she spoke to him as to her first sweetheart... all this dazed him, tempted him, intoxicated him, set a vehement pulse beating in his strong heart, a shiver almost of terror in his excited veins, a kind of torment in his rough nerves, whose every perversity he savored slowly.

In her truly lay forbidden possession, the joy that was not to be known, the crime and the supreme voluptuous pleasure.

When she spoke to him of love, he would have liked, in turn, to answer her: “Yes, I love you! You are the first I love, the only one I shall ever be able to love... You stir a great tempest within me that intoxicates me...” But he was ashamed of this, and the words that resounded within him seemed impossible to utter. So he remained silent, leaving it to her to speak—to her, since she was almost a child, a little child, and could say anything.

But merely in calling to her, in speaking to her, in uttering her name, he put an infinite love. It was no longer merely his desire for her, that vehement desire which had assailed him, enslaving him and twisting him to the point of pain; now it was something more, a kind of sadness, a pent-up and murky frenzy that possessed him to his innermost depths and wounded him like a thorn driven into his heart.

He, who had never faced his own conscience, was now afraid of himself. He feared something obscure; between him and her there was an indefinable, unknown force that terrified him; over his guilty love there hung something like a more-than-human threat. He wanted to be harsh, and could only manage to be gentle; he wanted not to look at her, and his eyes, despite himself, went to meet hers. Even when he was far away and distracted, her image remained fixed in his mind without respite. He wanted to think of other women, other loves, and she furtively nestled in his arms with a stronger promise; he wanted to thrust her away from him, as though to purify himself of this guilt, and the guilt came back to him, flowed into his heart through every vein, like a wave of voluptuous pleasure.

The little horse trotted on; the uniform countryside rested from the day’s labor, broken by farmhouses, crossed by roads, marked by hedges. A row of poplars here and there, across the vaporous plain, receded out of sight into the white night. Behind them the city loomed, overhung by a reddish glow which, in the still air, was the reflection of its many lights.

Beyond a hedge they saw a flock of sheep spending the night; it had spread across the little meadow in small groups, and slept there, gleaming white. The dog rushed to the verge, its fur all bristling, and barked.

“Look,” Loretta said with childlike wonder, “look how white they are and how close together they sleep.”

Those sleeping little sheep inspired a singular tenderness in her child’s heart. She added:

“Life in the country must be better than in the cities. Why don’t you take me away, Rigo?”

“Take you away? But where?”

“It doesn’t matter where. Just for one week. I should like to take a little journey with you, to stay close to you always, day and night, never to leave you, day and night... What happiness—just think!”

Her brother shook his head and, without speaking, caressed the backs of her hands, then her knees.

“Take me away...” she said again, pleadingly.

“It cannot be done.”

At that moment they passed a merry party returning to the city singing. A village appeared in the distance, and, before the village, behind a house, a cluster of thick trees where many lights shone.

“You see: that is where we are dining,” Arrigo said, pointing to the glow. “Many people come in summer because the food is good there.”
